---
title: "Where Machines Fail"
---

::: {.quest-dialog}
- **Goal:** you will sort jobs into "ask the model" and "run a script", and name the other ways a model fails with one mitigation each.
- **Before you start:** [Tokens, Not Letters](tokens-not-letters.html).
- **Time:** about 15 minutes.
:::

A language model is good at some jobs and bad at others. The skill is knowing which is which before you trust the output. Using a model is always your choice. This quest shows where the risk sits if you do.

## Good jobs: the result is checkable

Use a model where you can read the result, or run it, and judge it yourself:

- summarising text
- drafting prose, such as a README or a methods first draft
- explaining code or an error message
- converting formats, for example a samplesheet CSV to JSON (a structured text format)
- first drafts of code that you will then test

Summaries can leave things out or bend them. Spot-check against the source: numbers, gene and sample names, direction of effect, negations. Omissions are harder to see, so skim the abstract and limitations yourself. Ask the model to quote the supporting lines first, then summarise.

## Bad job: exact counting and arithmetic

Ask a model: "How many n are in banana?" The right answer is 2 (b-a-n-a-n-a). A model can get this wrong, and can be wrong while sounding sure.

Researchers disagree on why. One explanation is that the model reads tokens, which are chunks of letters. One study finds word length and the true count matter more than tokenisation. The fix works whichever cause is right.

The fix is to run a script:

```bash
echo banana | grep -o n | wc -l
```

It prints `2`. The macOS `wc` pads the number with spaces; the number is 2. A model asked to write Python for a counting task does better than a model asked to answer it directly. So for exact counts, have the model **write the script** and read the script and its output. Treat a count it states from "doing the sum in its head" as a guess to check.

The bioinformatics versions of the same trap:

| You want | Give it to |
|---|---|
| Number of sequences in a FASTA | `grep -c '>' file.fa`, or `seqkit stats` |
| GC content, read length statistics | a script, run by the agent, with the code visible |
| A p-value or any test statistic | a stats library in a script you can read and re-run |
| Sum or mean of a column | `awk`, or a script that prints the number |

Rule of thumb: ask for the command and its output, and treat a count stated in prose as a guess to check.

::: {.panel-tabset group="companion"}

## Claude Code

It can run Bash (the shell command tool) and write scripts, so ask: "write and run a command for this, and show me both the command and its output."

## OpenCode + Ollama

Same rule: ask for a script, and read the command and its output. Try the banana example with your own model to see how it does.

:::

## Other ways it fails

- **Hallucination:** a confident statement that is false, such as a plausible DOI, gene ID or tool flag that does not exist. Allow "I don't know", ask for word-for-word quotes first, restrict the model to supplied documents, and look up every ID in PubMed or Ensembl or run the tool's `--help`.
- **Sycophancy:** telling you what you want to hear. The model agrees with your wrong hypothesis, or softens a correct criticism when you push back. Ask for the strongest case against your idea, and hold back your preferred answer.
- **Long-context degradation:** accuracy and recall drop as input grows ("context rot"), and relevant text in the middle is used less. Curate the input (head, counts, filtered tables) and start fresh for a new task.
- **Instruction drift:** an early instruction is forgotten, for example after compaction (the harness replacing old conversation with a summary to free room). Keep a short instructions file (`CLAUDE.md` or similar, loaded at session start) and use a hook (a script the harness runs at set moments) for must-never rules.
- **Non-determinism:** the same prompt may give different answers, so run it twice and compare. Record the command, model and version, and treat the script the model wrote as the reproducible part.
- **Overconfidence:** the model reports a task as done while it is unfinished, often because it had no way to check. Give it a check to run (tests, row counts, md5) and read the output.
- **Prompt injection:** text from fetched content that the model treats as an instruction, for example a README, PDF or FASTA header that contains instructions the agent follows. Treat fetched content as data, review commands before approving them, and remember no system is fully immune.
- **Stale knowledge:** newer tool versions or database releases postdate the model's training. Check `--version` and the current docs. Current Claude models list a June 2026 training cutoff.

## The decision rule

Ask yourself: can I check the result cheaply and independently? If yes, ask the model: a bad answer is likely to show (omissions may not, so check those deliberately). If the answer must be exactly right and cannot be checked, use a script.

## Bonus

<div data-ao-honour="count-letter" data-xp="20">Ask a model to count one letter in a long word (or a mock 40-letter DNA string), then check it with <code>grep -o</code> and <code>wc -l</code>. Note whether it was right, and how sure it sounded. One try is a demonstration and falls short of proof.</div>
<div data-ao-honour="spot-check-summary" data-xp="20">Have a model summarise a methods paragraph you wrote. Check every number, name and negation against your original, and note anything omitted.</div>

## Lore

*Further reading. Optional.*

- [Lost in the Middle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172): Liu et al., arXiv, paper. Why read: it shows recall is best for text at the start or end of a long input and weaker in the middle. A preprint.
- [On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173): Maynez et al., ACL 2020, paper. Why read: it found hallucinated content in neural summaries; older models, but it shows why summaries need a spot check.
- [LLM The Genius Paradox: A Linguistic and Math Expert's Struggle with Simple Word-based Counting Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.14166): arXiv, paper. Why read: its abstract says specialised math and coding models still struggle with simple counting and that reasoning before answering is the most reliable fix; its full text adds that explicitly asking coding models for Python code worked. A preprint, not peer-reviewed as far as we checked.
- [Reduce hallucinations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/strengthen-guardrails/reduce-hallucinations): Anthropic, docs. Why read: it gives habits such as allowing "I don't know" and checking claims against quotes, the kind of fix for the confident-but-wrong rows in this quest; it says none removes errors.
:::
